newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo NBY changes reserve requirement regulation.
newsitem.headline: Yugo NBY changes reserve requirement regulation.

text.p: Yugoslavia's central bank changed its reserve requirement regulation by creating a new account for reserves giving Serbia and Montenegro more access to funds needed to finance their vital economic sectors.

Changes, published in the latest issue of the Official Gazette, include a 50-50 percent split in funds set aside for the reserve requirement to two separate accounts with the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY).
Fifty percent of the total reserve requirement transferred to the regular account can be used by a bank to bridge its daily liquidity problems.

But the other 50 percent of the reserve requirement will be transferred to a special account and can be invested in securities with maturity of up to six months and carry an interest rate equal to the NBY discount rate.
According to the NBY decision, banks can invest in various forms of commercial paper issued by the state-owned Serbian and Montenegrin commodity reserve agencies.
In the case of Serbia, funds will be used to finance stockpiling of produce harvested late in 1996.
As for Montenegro, money will finance preparations for the 1997 tourist season.
The NBY also said its Accounting and Payments Office will transfer funds from the regular to the special account until the special account reaches 50 percent of the total reserve requirement.
The new regulation will also oblige banks to deposit with the NBY 15 percent of money lent to other banks.
Banks currently transfer 15 percent of deposits to fulfill the central bank's reserve requirement.
The NBY said the changes would enable banks to lend more money to companies, but bankers said the new regulations would tighten their liquidity.
"The decisions apply for the period from February 28 to June 30, 1997. It is a trial period to find out if we can persuade banks to lend more to companies," a central bank official said.

"Previously, the reserve requirement did not apply to interbank activity. But we feel banks need to serve companies and not only act as dealers in their isolated interbank activities," said the official who declined to be named.
But bankers warned it could aggravate their liquidity problems.

"This is a fresh blow to banks' liquidity and now, even those who have money will think twice before they lend," head of the Trziste Novca brokerage Nikola Arandjelovic said. Reserve requirement regulation changes came only days after the NBY said it planned to reduce the reserve requirement to give commercial banks more scope to increase their credit activity. But NBY officials did not say when the planned cut would take place. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
